articles.title: Ecuador: la semi dictadura de Noboa busca ganar por eliminación de opositores, no por votos
articles.author: Pilar Troya Fernández
articles.content: Read in English here El presidente Daniel Noboa gobierna Ecuador con métodos cada vez más autoritarios. Elegido en 2023 y reelegido en 2025, ha concentrado poder en el Ejecutivo, chocado con la Corte Constitucional, abusado de los estados de excepción y convertido a la justicia en un instrumento contra sus adversarios. Analistas y organizaciones de derechos humanos describen una deriva filodictatorial: un mandatario que conserva las formas de la democracia mientras erosiona su contenido. La antesala de las elecciones de gobiernos locales del 29 de noviembre de 2026 ofrece el ejemplo más nítido de esa estrategia, dirigida a ganar con la estrategia de dejar sin candidaturas a la oposición. Una jugada en dos movimientos La maniobra combina dos piezas que solo se entienden juntas. La primera: el 6 de marzo de 2026, a partir de una denuncia de la Fiscalía, un juez del Tribunal Contencioso Electoral (TCE) suspendió por nueve meses a la Revolución Ciudadana (RC), el mayor partido opositor y movimiento del expresidente Rafael Correa. La medida fue ratificada semanas después y, en julio, avalada por la Corte Constitucional. Al mismo tiempo, Unidad Popular, partido de izquierda y Construye, movimiento de derecha por el que fue candidato presidencial Fernando Villavicencio, asesinado en 2023, fueron sacados del registro de organizaciones políticas por el Consejo Nacional Electoral (CNE) con el argumento de que no cumplían el número mínimo de afiliados que exige la ley. La apelación fue negada en el caso de Construye que denunció una “persecución judicial a críticos y opositores” y calificó la decisión de fraude democrático. Unidad Popular consiguió probar que el CNE actuó fuera del límite temporal legal (23 días tarde), y que la cancelación carecía de respaldo suficiente sobre el número real de afiliados. La segunda pieza es el calendario. En marzo, el Consejo Nacional Electoral (CNE) adelantó al 29 de noviembre de 2026 las elecciones de gobiernos locales previstas para febrero de 2027, alegando el riesgo de lluvias del Fenómeno del Niño; ni el Niño de 1998 ni la pandemia habían justificado antes un adelanto semejante. El efecto de encajar ambas piezas es preciso: el nuevo periodo de inscripción de candidaturas – del 2 al 17 de agosto de 2026 – cae dentro de los nueve meses en que la oposición está suspendida. Adelantar las elecciones para hacerlas coincidir con la suspensión impide que el principal rival del gobierno (RC) presente listas con su propia sigla. El partido alternativo, también clausurado Ante el bloqueo, el correísmo buscó una salida legal: inscribir a sus candidatos bajo el movimiento aliado Amigo. La alternativa duró poco. El 16 de julio, la Fiscalía informó al TCE de una investigación por presunto lavado de activos contra ese movimiento; al día siguiente, el Tribunal lo suspendió también por nueve meses, y el CNE ejecutó la medida de inmediato, apenas dos semanas antes del plazo de inscripción. La conducta del Ejecutivo alimenta las sospechas. El 23 de julio, Noboa afirmó que los precandidatos podían inscribirse por “cualquier otro partido que no se haya prestado para lavado de activos”, mencionando al Partido Socialista a la par, o sea presentando como hecho consumado un presunto delito que aún se investiga. Su secretario de la Administración Pública, José Julio Neira, exdirector de la unidad estatal que maneja la información financiera reservada, detalló en público el origen de las sospechas. El jurista Mauricio Alarcón advirtió que lo alarmante no es la investigación, sino que el gobierno parezca conocer expedientes reservados “que ni siquiera están en manos de los actores afectados”, y cuestionó “la selectividad” y la coincidencia con el calendario electoral. Si los candidatos de la RC se inscriben por el Partido Socialista, no sorprendería que este fuera también cancelado o suspendido. Tortura, desapariciones y activistas muertos Todo ocurre sobre un telón de fondo siniestro. En junio de 2026, Ecuador ingresó por primera vez en el Índice Global de Tortura de la Organización Mundial Contra la Tortura, en la categoría de “alto riesgo”: la entidad documentó 369 denuncias de tortura y al menos 51 desapariciones forzadas atribuidas a agentes estatales entre 2024 y 2026, en el marco del “conflicto armado interno” declarado por el gobierno, mismo que ha decretado 21 estados de excepción, 9 toques de queda y 272 días con restricción de movimientos con resultado casi nulo en reducción de la criminalidad y un aumento del desplazamiento interno por amenazas, extorsión y presiones de los grupos criminales. En ese clima se inscriben dos muertes. Robinson del Pezo, que cubría conflictos de tierras en la provincia de Santa Elena, fue asesinado en noviembre de 2025. La activista anticorrupción Mónica Silva, de origen polaco y radicada más de una década en el país, que había exigido justicia por ese crimen y denunciado amenazas contra su vida, fue hallada muerta el 8 de junio de 2026. El ministro del Interior sugirió un suicidio, pero la autopsia reveló un golpe en la cabeza y estrangulamiento. Silva investigaba presuntos envíos de cocaína ocultos en contenedores de banano de una empresa vinculada a la familia del presidente, y una red de tráfico de tierras. La relatora de la ONU para defensores de derechos humanos pidió a Ecuador “cesar la persecución” y proteger a los activistas. Corrupción casa adentro El discurso oficial presenta las causas contra la oposición como una cruzada anticorrupción. Sin embargo, el mayor escándalo del periodo salpica al propio Ejecutivo: en el caso Progen, la Contraloría General del Estado cifró en unos 104 millones de dólares el perjuicio al Estado por contratos de generación térmica de emergencia firmados en 2024 con esa empresa estadounidense, cuyos equipos nunca entraron en operación. Están además los ocho cargamentos de cocaína encontrados en las exportaciones de banano de la familia Noboa. El resultado es una elección cuyos contendientes se definen en los tribunales antes que en las urnas. El gobierno insiste en que se trata de causas ajenas al Ejecutivo; la oposición y parte de la comunidad jurídica replican que la selectividad de los procesos y su oportuno calendario apuntan en otra dirección. Pilar Troya Fernández es ecuatoriana, antropóloga con maestría en estudios de género e investigadora del Instituto Tricontinental de Investigación Social . Fue asesora de la Secretaría Nacional de Planificación, asesora de la Secretaría Nacional de Educación Superior, Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación y Subsecretaria General de Educación Superior en Ecuador. Actualmente reside en Brasil. Este artículo fue producido por Globetrotter .

articles.title: “Zero Accountability”: Ecuadorian Prosecutor Assassinated While Investigating U.S. Boat Strikes
articles.content: U.S. boat strikes across the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have killed at least 221 people since September, while the Trump administration has provided no evidence linking the vessels or their passengers to drug trafficking. Ecuadorian prosecutor Alexandra Bravo was fatally shot on June 14 by a hitman in the city of Manta. Bravo had been investigating U.S. strikes on three Ecuadorian boats in which 36 passengers survived, many of them recounting alleged torture by American gunmen in U.S. military uniforms aboard a U.S.-flagged patrol ship. The allegations of U.S. boat strikes and torture Bravo was investigating “are a reflection of the growing U.S.-backed military dictatorship in Ecuador,” says Camila Lourdes Galarza, an investigative journalist and labor organizer based in Quito. Lourdes Galarza says that during Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s reelection last year, former Blackwater mercenaries patrolled voting sites at gunpoint. “The Trump administration has deepened U.S. security cooperation with Ecuador as a response to the surge in violence in [Ecuador], particularly to the growth of organized crime groups,” adds Juanita Goebertus, director of the Americas division at Human Rights Watch. “None of the two governments have provided transparency about the nature of their security cooperation.”

articles.title: India’s Cockroach Rebellion and what comes next
articles.author: Atul Chandra
articles.content: They came to Jantar Mantar in cockroach masks, throwing back at power a word that power had used against them. On July 25, 2026, after weeks of protest, a twenty-six-day hunger strike by Sonam Wangchuk, baton charges, tear gas and the closure of 18 Delhi Metro stations, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan submitted his resignation . By late afternoon on July 25, India’s students and young people had forced one of the cabinet’s most powerful figures from office. Who are the cockroaches? On May 15, 2026, during a Supreme Court session, the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, described the unemployed youth who ‘attack institutions’ as “youngsters like cockroaches”. The comment sparked anger amongst young people, and a creative response: the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party, a place for the young “cockroaches” to come together and organize their rejection of the system. Within twenty-four hours of its formation, the Cockroach Janta Party generated unprecedented momentum. Founded on May 16, 2026 as a digital clapback to the judge’s jibe, the Cockroach Janta Party drew over twenty million online followers within a fortnight. But, it did not just accumulate followers. It published manifestos on different aspects of Indian political life, such as how Chief Justices are appointed, what electoral integrity should be, demands for media that is free and independent from corporate houses like Adani and Ambani, and on the national examination system. The CJP ran a nationwide “Pradhan Go Back” campaign centered around an indefinite sit-in at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi. As part of the sit-in, several activists were on hunger strike, including Sonam Wangchuk who sustained his hunger strike for 26 days. The youth and student movement also organized a mass mobilization of tens of thousands to march to Parliament on July 20, 2026. In just two months, it forced a breakthrough that had eluded even the most resilient peasant and farmers movements, human rights advocates, independent journalists, and opposition groups over a decade of struggle. The weight of that should be neither understated nor misread. For twelve years the Modi government has treated concessions as weakness. It outlasted the largest farmers’ mobilization in the country’s history, and when it repealed the three farm laws in November 2021 it kept its agriculture minister in place to pilot the repeal himself. It absorbed the anti-CAA protests, the female wrestlers’ sit-in ,and the agony of Manipur without losing a minister. Pradhan, only weeks earlier, had called the students “a B-team of terrorists” out to “divide the country”, a charge sharpened by his own past: he entered politics protesting a paper leak in 1997. That a government so practiced in refusal has given up a cabinet post marks a genuine shift in the balance of forces. The long apprenticeship of Indian democracy The young have carried this burden before. India’s students have repeatedly tested whether the republic’s promises mean anything, and each time expanded them. When the colonial state partitioned Bengal in 1905, students tore up the circular threatening them, walked out of government colleges, and built a parallel “national education” that survives today. When Gandhi called for non-cooperation in 1920, they emptied the Raj’s classrooms and founded Jamia Millia Islamia. In 1942, with the Congress leadership in jail, it was students who hoisted flags over secretariats and ran Usha Mehta’s underground Congress Radio. After independence, the pattern deepened into something more than protest. In 1965, students across Tamil Nadu rose up against the imposition of Hindi. The state killed scores of them, then reversed its language policy and lost two Union ministers from the region. In the winter of 1973 to 1974, a hostel fee rise in Ahmedabad became the Nav Nirman Andolan, which forced out Gujarat’s chief minister Chimanbhai Patel and dissolved the assembly. That current ran to Bihar, where a student agitation drew in Jayaprakash Narayan, hardened into the movement Indira Gandhi answered with the Emergency, and returned in 1977 to remove her. A student union led the Assam agitation of 1979 to 1985 and compelled a national government to sign an accord ; Osmania University’s students were central to the birth of Telangana in 2014. None of this was won by decorum but by pressure, by forcing the state to answer to people it preferred to ignore. That is what deepening a democracy means. The visible concession and the structural test Here the sober reading begins. Across all these cases runs a single pattern: the state gives up the visible while the structural becomes the real terrain of contest. The anti-CAA and NRC protests of 2019 and 2020 imposed a real cost. The nationwide National Register of Citizens was shelved and has not been developed, while the government is still telling Parliament that no decision has been taken. Yet the Citizenship Amendment Act itself was passed and its rules notified in March 2024. The movement won a pause, not a repeal. Pradhan’s exit sits inside this same logic, and the government has moved quickly to be seen taking action. In the days around the resignation, the Union Cabinet cleared a tougher anti-paper-leak bill, doubling prison terms and raising fines to ten crore rupees, with fast-track trials promised within three months, while the National Testing Agency dismissed forty-seven officials and announced an overhaul of its outsourcing model. So far, the measures taken are focused on punishment and personnel, aimed at those who breach the system rather than the system that produces the breach. Whether the promised overhaul delivers a meaningfully new structure, or refurbishes the same commodified examination process that turns the futures of millions into a market of coaching fees and leaked papers, is precisely what remains to be seen. While student leaders have now called off the protests at Jantar Mantar after securing government commitments to drop police cases and compensate affected families, the retreat from the streets is best understood not as the final settlement of a grievance, but as a conditional pause – leaving the broader account of structural reform still waiting to be drawn up. Unity is the real target What made the victory possible also marks its point of greatest vulnerability. Its strength lay in a solidarity that cut across the lines ordinarily used to fragment popular anger, a constituency defined not by caste, faith or region but by a shared material condition: the cheated aspirant, the graduate without work, the family that mortgaged land for a coaching fee. Grievances of that kind belong to everyone at once, which is why they unsettle a government fluent in communal arithmetic. The record shows how such unity dissolves. In 1990 the mobilization against the Mandal Commission’s reservations (also known as Other Backward Caste reservations) split the student body along caste lines, upper-caste youth against the quota, Bahujan youth for it, and the common antagonist, an unaccountable state, slipped from view. The Assam movement built a formidable unity, but on an ethnic and exclusionary basis that ended in the massacre of some 2,000 Bengali Muslims at Nellie in Assam. The instrument that breaks a movement of this kind is rarely the baton. It is the reminder to students that they are Hindu or Muslim, forward or backward, before they are the exploited youth. Pradhan’s charge that the protesters sought to “divide the country” inverts the real danger, which is that the country’s rulers divide the protest. The apparatus that met them remains where it was. The lathis, the tear gas, the internet shutdown near Parliament, the facial-recognition cameras, and the automatic weapons at its gates were withdrawn only when the political cost of using them grew too high. A concession extracted under pressure lasts only as long as the pressure stays credible. None of this diminishes the achievement. For the first time in twelve years an administration built on the appearance of invulnerability has been made to retreat by ordinary people standing together. But a retreat is not a rout, and a resignation is not a reckoning. The students have shown that the state can be moved. Whether it can be changed will be settled not at the moment of a minister’s exit but in the far longer contest over the structures left behind. Atul Chandra is the Asia Co-Coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research.

articles.title: Keiko Fujimori takes office as Peru’s new president
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: On July 28, right-wing candidate Keiko Fujimori took office as president of Peru. After being defeated three times in a row (2016, 2021, and 2022), Fujimori managed to secure a victory that had eluded her until now due to the significant resistance caused by the figure of her father, Alberto Fujimori , who ruled Peru through a combination of an iron fist and the rapid implementation of the most predatory neoliberalism throughout the 1990s and proclaimed himself a dictator. Paradoxically, Keiko Fujimori has simultaneously used her father’s legacy as a political springboard; for while it provokes widespread rejection, it also guarantees a loyal voter base known as “Fujimorism,” which has enabled her to reach the runoff election four times, including in 2026. A recent history of instability But this year, things seem to have finally gone her way. After a vote count marred by controversy, allegations of electoral fraud, rule changes, and heated exchanges, Fujimori was declared president-elect over Roberto Sánchez. The leftist candidate was backed by Pedro Castillo, Peru’s former president, who is currently in prison for attempting to convene a Constituent Assembly. The opposition, including Fujimori’s supporters, labeled the move an attempted coup. Following this, Peru was plunged into a wave of protests demanding the resignation of Dina Boluarte’s government. Boluarte, the country’s new president, did not hesitate to harshly suppress the months-long demonstrations, leaving more than 50 dead; as a result, Boluarte is now facing a criminal investigation for alleged human rights violations. Boluarte was subsequently succeeded by several interim presidents whose brief tenures merely underscored the clear political crisis the country is facing. And it is, in fact, a crisis of legitimacy that Fujimori must now overcome. In the first round, her vote share did not exceed 17.19%. In the runoff, she secured a (highly contested) victory with just 50.14% to 49.86%. Her victory was by a margin of barely 50,000 votes. Sánchez managed to secure nearly 50% of the vote share thanks to the support of part of the center and even many right-wingers who were willing to negotiate with the left rather than face a government led by a new Fujimori. Unity and neoliberalism However, beyond the allegations of electoral fraud and the civil resistance that Sánchez has promised, the fact is that Fujimori was sworn in on July 28. She is the new president of a country that, despite its constant political crises, remains economically stable. However, many critics of the current neoliberal system argue that it is a system that benefits international capital (which holds a strong position in the Peruvian economy) and the country’s wealthiest but keeps the vast majority of Peruvians in poverty, informal employment, and material insecurity. Fujimori, 51, as she stated in her inaugural address , did not promise to transform Peru’s neoliberal model, but rather to reinforce it. To do so, the new president does not appear to wish to disrupt the economic functioning of Peruvian neoliberalism, but rather to secure the other leg of the table needed to maintain stability: the political situation. At least that is what she hinted at in her speech: “I am committed to achieving the goals of order and national reconciliation, in perfectly compatible terms. The real enemies are Peru’s major and serious problems.” Clearly, Keiko is seeking to secure, as soon as possible, a sort of truce among Peruvian political groups that, in recent years, have been marked by relentless conflict. To this end, Fujimori has established two areas of focus that she hopes will earn her greater legitimacy from her opponents: crime and natural disasters. “The fight will not be limited to common criminals. We will go after the national and international mafias that finance extortion, contract killings, drug trafficking, and illegal mining,” said Fujimori , while also stating that the Armed Forces will assume new responsibilities for internal security and promising to improve the National Police’s equipment. According to the president , nearly 24% of companies in Peru have been subjected to extortion by criminal groups. She also promised to tackle the upcoming El Niño phenomenon with intelligence and planning; according to some experts, it could become the most devastating natural disaster of its kind in decades. For this reason, Fujimori announced that she is elevating this issue to a “national emergency,” on par with the fight against crime. Likewise, Fujimori, like the other newly elected presidents, kept a trump card up her sleeve in case she needed it. She stated that Peru’s situation is complex and painful. “We inherited a state weakened by corruption.” She even went so far as to describe the country’s situation as “catastrophic” due to inadequate basic services, thousands of stalled public works projects, and a “chaotic” transportation system – all resulting from “decades of governments that shirked their responsibilities.” Thus, Fujimori decided to begin her term with a somewhat cautious speech, yet one that signaled her readiness to launch a new phase in the development of neoliberalism in Peru. And this cannot be separated from the region’s current geopolitical context. With the victories of Fujimori in Peru and De la Espriella in Colombia, the ideological balance of these governments is clearly shifting toward a right wing aligned with Washington’s agenda. A clear yet complex shift to the right It comes as no surprise to see right-wing and far-right presidents in the front row during Fujimori’s speech: Nasry Asfura of Honduras, Daniel Noboa of Ecuador, José Raúl Mulino of Panama, Santiago Peña of Paraguay, Rodrigo Paz of Bolivia, José Antonio Kast of Chile, and Javier Milei of Argentina – all of whom have signed the Shield of the Americas, the new hemispheric strategy led by the Trump administration. Thus, with only Yamandú Orsi, Uruguay’s president, representing the center-left in attendance at the presidential inauguration in Lima, the region’s clear shift to the right was evident. Perhaps the most notable absence was that of Brazil’s center-left President Lula da Silva (a country with which Peru shares a border of more than 2,800 kilometers) who declined to attend both Fujimori’s inauguration and that of De la Espriella, scheduled for next month. However, Fujimori will face a dilemma similar to that of Kast. While they may align politically with Washington, Peru’s main trading partner is China, a country that recently inaugurated the massive Chancay seaport, which promises to become the primary gateway for Chinese products into South America via the Pacific Ocean. For now, Fujimori has maintained a pragmatic stance on economic matters and has instead focused on restoring the legitimacy of a political system whose state of near-perpetual crisis has become the norm – a situation that could cause significant difficulties for a newly inaugurated government, which marks the ninth administration in just 10 years. To that end, she announced an increase in the minimum wage to $381 (1,300 soles) and compensation for companies, signaling that her administration is kicking off with executive orders. “From this moment on, an irreversible countdown begins. We have 1,826 days of administration ahead of us, during which every ministry, every region, and every public official will have to work intensely, with measurable goals and constant accountability.” Keiko Fujimori is Peru’s first female president, a fact that has been celebrated by many. However, her most important challenge now will be to prove that she can be the first female president to successfully complete her term since 2016. For now, she has Congress’s support, although if recent Peruvian political history has taught us anything, it is that nothing is more fragile than the apparent certainty of power.
